scant

SKANT -- one syllable, rhymes with 'plant'. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Scant is barely sufficient or adequate.

The detective refused to charge anyone on such scant evidence -- a single blurry photo and one secondhand rumor.

Example

The relief team opens the last supply crate to find scant provisions: just two boxes of bandages and a half-empty bottle of antiseptic for an entire village.

Two boxes of bandages for a whole village fall far short of what is needed. Scant describes an amount that is barely sufficient -- there is some, but not nearly enough to cover the need.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

meager: Meager means small and inadequate in amount, with a note of thinness or poverty about it -- a meager salary, a meager meal. Meager always disappoints, while scant measures an amount against a mark and finds it just barely there: scant evidence is almost, but not quite, enough.

scarce: Scarce means hard to come by at all -- water is scarce in a desert, and tickets grow scarce as a show sells out. Scarce describes supply in the wider world, while scant describes the amount in hand: your evidence can be scant even when evidence generally is plentiful.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

abundant: existing in large quantities

ample: more than enough

Where it sits · how harshly the shortage is felt — insufficient → scant → paltry

insufficient vs. scant: Insufficient is the flat, clinical cousin of scant -- it simply reports that there is not enough, while scant adds a wince: the amount is so small you feel the shortage.

paltry vs. scant: Paltry is harsher than scant: scant rainfall is barely enough for the crops, while a paltry donation is so meager it invites scorn.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — skamm-/scant

root — skamm-/scant: short, brief (Old Norse skammt, from skammr 'short')

Put it together

Put it together: Scant comes from Old Norse skammt, 'short,' brought to England by Norse settlers a thousand years ago. An amount that is scant has been cut short -- measured out so briefly that it barely covers the need.

Use the root in a new word: scanty

Use the root in a new word: scanty: The stranded sailors stretched their scanty rations across two extra days.

Word Building

Word Choice

Scant sits before nouns of quantity: scant evidence, scant resources, scant attention, scant rainfall. It is about amount -- how much there is -- and it always implies the amount falls short. Cooks use it for measurements too: 'a scant teaspoon' means just barely a teaspoon, not a drop more.
